metadata.title: THE ROLE OF SUBNATIONAL GOVERNMENTS IN ADULT SKILLS SYSTEMS: TÜRKIYE

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD country note does not analyze student-level ILSA microdata and therefore does not define a sampling frame, student-level analytic sample, or any plausible-value (PV) based achievement outcomes. The document describes governance structures and allocation of responsibilities/expenditure across national, regional, and local levels for Türkiye’s adult skills system. As a result, there are no survey weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT) or replicate-weight schemes (e.g., BRR/jackknife) to apply. For any future empirical work using ILSA microdata, analysts should use the official ILSA sampling weights and PV procedures provided by the data provider; however, this note itself is descriptive policy mapping rather than an assessment-based statistical analysis.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because this document is a governance and responsibilities overview of Türkiye’s adult skills system, not an analysis of cognitive assessment outcomes from an ILSA (e.g., PISA/TIMSS/PIRLS/PIAAC) with PV-based achievement scores. Missing-data handling is not reported because there is no student-level dataset construction, estimation model, or imputation/deletion procedure described; the tables summarize institutional responsibilities and expenditure shares compiled from available information.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used a policy/governance compilation approach for Türkiye’s adult skills system; no student-level assessment dataset or analytic subsample is defined in the note.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD Türkiye country note provides a descriptive overview of how the adult skills system is governed across national, regional, and local levels. It reports governance centralisation, the leading role of the central government, and the allocation of responsibilities across policy areas (VET, HVET, CET, adult education, and ALMP) using tables that indicate which level performs strategy, intelligence, implementation, funding, and delivery. The note also quantifies the subnational share of general government expenditure (8.4%) and describes key institutions (e.g., Ministry of National Education, Council of Higher Education, Ministry of Labour and Social Security/PES, and provincial/local bodies). Because it is not an assessment-based empirical study, it does not use ILSA microdata, plausible values, or statistical modeling benchmarks, and it does not evaluate predictive performance. The implication is primarily institutional: strengthening coordination mechanisms and clarifying responsibilities across levels may improve adult-skills service delivery and alignment with regional labour-market needs.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is sparse with respect to ML and assessment methodology because the document is a policy country note rather than an empirical large-scale assessment analysis. There is no student sample, no assessment domain, and no model-based outcome; consequently, fields such as total_students, PV handling, missing-data handling, and main_findings are not applicable in the ILSA/ML sense. The tables function as governance mapping rather than statistical results.
